data: How did life first arise on Planet Earth 4 billion years ago? In this course, which comprises both organismal and molecular evolution, we will begin with early theories of evolution that lead up to Darwin and Wallace's theory of natural selection. We thus gain insight into the process of scientific inquiry that resulted in one of the most important theories in the biological sciences, before concluding by integrating it with Mendel's theory of genetics referred to as the Evolutionary Synthesis. The course will look at the evidence of macro and micro evolutionary processes, and the evolution of plants and animals to understand the basis of the diversity of living organisms on Earth. Through numerous examples, students will learn about adaptive strategies at the level of individual organisms that may underlie evolutionary changes at the level of a population. At a molecular level, we trace the evolution of life, starting from self-replicating molecules, to the RNA world, to the evolution of cellular components. Along the way we will discuss the role played by the constituent molecules of life. We will discuss the origin of the field of molecular genetics from the Evolutionary Synthesis, bringing the disparate fields of evolutionary biology and genetics together. We will discuss the development and employment of the molecular clock and the salience of neutral mutations in establishing relatedness among organisms, using such markers as mitochondrial, chloroplast, ribosomal and nuclear genetic material, aided considerably by such technological advancements as protein electrophoresis, leading to the amplification of DNA using the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for whole genome sequencing. This course will briefly discuss how the sequence information comes together with the current computational power to draw the phylogenetic tree of life.
